newsitem.title: INDIA: Worst India crash devastates once peaceful fields.
newsitem.headline: Worst India crash devastates once peaceful fields.

text.p: Charred and mangled bodies littered once peaceful fields in this rural area of north India on Wednesday after the world's worst mid-air collision.
Dozens of corpses, including those of children, lay strewn around the main crash site of the smouldering remains of the Saudi Arabian Airlines Boeing 747.
The stench of burnt human flesh mingled with the smell of burning rubber, chemicals and plastic hung over the crash site.
The macabre scene included airline dinner trays with curries on trolleys and crockery for meals that were never served.
Suitcases, some open and empty, were also strewn on the ground, over which police, rescue teams and reporters tried to tread gingerly to avoid trampling on bodies.
Local people said there had been looting. "It's very sad that people here behave in this manner," local businessman Vinod Garg told Reuters.
First light on Wednesday revealed terrible scenes of chaos and destruction after what was also India's worst air disaster.
Nearly 14 hours after the collision, firemen were still trying to douse smouldering parts of the jumbo jet, especially the fuselage which had its top torn away.
About 10 km (six miles) away, also on farmland, lay the shattered remains of the other aircraft, a Kazakh Ilyushin Il-76 cargo plane.
Officials said the two aircraft collided at a height of about 15,000 feet (4,570 metres) some seven minutes after the Saudi jumbo had left New Delhi airport and the Ilyushin was descending.
All 350 people aboard the two aircraft died, officials believe. More than 200 bodies were recovered overnight.
At one point, officials said three or four survivors were pulled from the mass of wreckage but died on the way to hospital near Charkhi Dadri, which has an estimated population of 50,000 people.
Witnesses said the aircraft plunged to earth, some 80 km (50 miles) from New Delhi, like twin fireballs after the night collision.
An American military pilot said he saw a bright light in the sky which he initially took to be lightning as he prepared to land at Delhi's Indira Gandhi airport.
Then he saw two fireballs descending to earth.
"We have seen nothing like this before," said one rescue worker, with a white handkerchief covering his face. "It is bizarre and sickening."
Police official V. B. Singh told Reuters, "Our first priority is to look for survivors, of which there is very little hope".
